## What you should be able to do by Friday

- Apply the temporary-and-unique test to real work, and name the cases where it returns the wrong answer.
- State the iron triangle and give three specific reasons it misleads.
- Score a project on five dimensions of success and defend the score that will be contested.
- Tell a standard, a method, guidance and a framework apart, and say which one you could sue over.
- Choose between an adaptive and a predictive approach using five questions rather than a preference.

## Notes

### 1 · What counts as a project

A project is a temporary endeavour undertaken to create a unique product, service, or result. Two
words carry the load: *temporary* (a definite start and end — bounded, not brief) and *unique* (not
previously produced in this exact configuration). Operations are ongoing and repetitive.

The distinction earns its keep because the techniques differ. Operations optimize a known process;
projects execute an unrepeated one under uncertainty. Variance is the enemy of a production line.
The thing nobody thought of is the enemy of a project.

Then there are the cases where the test returns an unhelpful answer. A film production is temporary
and unique — but the studio makes one every year. A software release train ships something unique
each time on an operational cadence. A refinery maintenance shutdown recurs on a schedule and is
still planned as a project every time.

The conclusion to take from those is not that the definition is broken. It is that **project versus
operation is a choice about which toolkit to apply**, not a fact about the world. Someone decides,
and the decision has consequences you can predict.

::: {.roommate}
#### Roommate link

**Cooking a dinner party vs. running a restaurant.** The dinner party is a project — fixed date,
unique menu, guests who will remember it. The restaurant is operations. A chef who runs a restaurant
well can still fail at a dinner party, because the failure modes differ: the restaurant's enemy is
variance, the dinner party's is the thing you forgot to buy.
:::

### 2 · Why the iron triangle is not a success model

Scope–time–cost, with quality either inside the triangle or floating above it. It fails in three
specific ways.

1. **It is a constraint model, not a success model.** Meeting all three says nothing about whether
   the output was worth building. The Sydney Opera House was estimated at A$7M and cost A$102M —
   over 1,300% over — and opened in 1973 against a scheduled 1963 completion. Nobody remembers it
   as a failure.
2. **It hides the asymmetry between the legs.** They are not interchangeable. Scope is usually the
   only one anyone will actually flex, and the flex usually goes unacknowledged.
3. **It has no stakeholder dimension.** The person who paid, the person who uses it, and the team
   who built it can disagree about success, and routinely do.

### 3 · How success is actually measured

Shenhar & Dvir's five dimensions, from *Reinventing Project Management* (2007). The 2001
*Long Range Planning* paper has only four — *impact on the team* was added in the book.

| Dimension | Question | Time horizon |
|---|---|---|
| Project efficiency | Did we hit time and budget? | Immediate |
| Impact on customer | Does it meet requirements and get used? | Months |
| Impact on team | Did the team grow, or burn out? | Months |
| Business/direct success | Did it produce commercial or mission value? | 1–2 years |
| Preparing for the future | Did it create capability, technology, or market position? | 3–5 years |

Notice what the time horizons do to incentives. The dimension available on the day a project closes
is the dimension you get judged on; the ones that would vindicate or condemn you arrive after
everyone has moved on.

This model is also what makes the agile-versus-predictive evidence legible. Gemino et al. (2021)
found agile and hybrid approaches improved *stakeholder* success over traditional while achieving
statistically **the same** budget, time, scope and quality outcomes. Measure only the iron triangle
and you conclude approach doesn't matter. That conclusion is a measurement artifact.

### 4 · The evidence, and why it argues with itself

Flyvbjerg's database of more than 16,000 projects: **0.5%** come in on budget, on time, and with the
promised benefits. **8.5%** hit budget and schedule. Mean cost overrun by category — nuclear waste
storage +238%, Olympic Games +157%, nuclear power +120%, IT +73%, buildings +62%, rail +39%,
tunnels +37%, wind +13%, solar +1%.

Now complicate it. Chapman (2024), *Project Management Journal* 55(6), examined 228 road and 96 rail
projects in Sweden and found a typical road cost overrun of **2.7%** and a rail **1.8% underrun**,
with 93% of road and 70% of rail projects achieving their intended benefits. Chapman (2025),
*International Journal of Project Management* 43(8) 102787, extended this to 125 rail and 280 road
projects across Denmark, Norway and Sweden, 2008–2022, and found them delivered **on cost, over
time**, with no evidence of systematic optimism bias or strategic misrepresentation.

Both cannot be a universal law. **Base rates are not constants of nature; they are properties of a
governance regime.** Before you repeat a failure statistic, you need to know which regime produced
it.

### 5 · The standards landscape

**PMBOK Guide, Eighth Edition** (PMI — released late 2025, general availability January 2026):

- **Six principles**, down from twelve in the 7th edition: adopt a holistic view; focus on value;
  embed quality into processes and deliverables; be an accountable leader; integrate sustainability
  across all project areas; build an empowered culture. Sustainability is newly *standalone* — in
  the 7th edition it sat inside Stewardship rather than carrying its own principle.
- **Seven performance domains**, down from eight: Governance, Scope, Schedule, Finance,
  Stakeholders, Resources, Risk.
- **40 processes**, reintroduced in deliberately non-prescriptive form, consolidated from the 49 in
  the 2022 *Process Groups: A Practice Guide*.
- Expanded material on AI, PMO roles, and procurement.

The interesting part is the oscillation. PMBOK 6 (2017) was process-heavy — 49 processes, five
process groups, ten knowledge areas. PMBOK 7 (2021) threw the processes out and went principle-based.
PMBOK 8 (2025) brought them back, framed as non-prescriptive. Read that trajectory as a finding: pure
principles gave practitioners nothing to *do*, pure processes gave them nothing to *think with*, and
the 8th edition is an attempt to hold both.

The other three, in a line each:

| Standard | What it claims to be | Governance stance |
|---|---|---|
| PMBOK 8 (PMI, 2025–26) | A body of knowledge + a standard; descriptive | Tailoring is mandatory |
| PRINCE2 (AXELOS/PeopleCert) | A *method* — prescriptive processes and roles | Strong: project board, stage boundaries, exception management |
| ISO 21502:2020 | Guidance, deliberately generic and vendor-neutral | Light; designed to be referenced in contracts |
| Scrum Guide (Nov 2020) | A *framework*, immutable, deliberately incomplete | None beyond the team; explicitly silent on portfolio |

**The Scrum Guide is 13 pages and has not been revised since November 2020.** Standards are widely
assumed to churn; this one does not. Scrum.org's position is that it is updated rarely by design.
The 2020 revision removed prescriptive language to make it "minimally sufficient," added the Product
Goal, and gave each of the three artifacts one commitment — Product Backlog → Product Goal, Sprint
Backlog → Sprint Goal, Increment → Definition of Done.

::: {.roommate}
#### Roommate link

**Building codes vs. architectural style.** A building code is prescriptive, legally enforceable,
and says nothing about whether the building is good. A style is a set of principles a designer can
violate deliberately. PRINCE2 is closer to a code; PMBOK 7/8 is closer to a style guide; Scrum is
closer to a poetic form — a sonnet is 14 lines, and the constraint is the point.
:::

### 6 · Tailoring — five questions, every time

Run these on every project in this course, starting with your final project:

1. How much will requirements change between now and delivery? *(High → adaptive)*
2. How expensive is a late change? *(Very expensive → predictive front-loading)*
3. Can we deliver value in increments a stakeholder would actually accept? *(No → predictive)*
4. Is there a regulatory or contractual gate that requires a frozen baseline? *(Yes → predictive at least at the gate)*
5. Is the team co-located enough, and empowered enough, for self-management? *(No → the agile ceremonies will be theatre)*

## Work with AI on this week

Three roles, three different jobs. See [AI Studio](../ai.qmd) for the full loop and the exact prompts.

::: {.tutor}
### Tutor check — one question at a time, no lecturing

1. A vendor tells you 71% of software projects fail. What would you need to know before repeating that number?
2. Your project finished 20% over budget and the client renewed for three more years. Did it succeed?
3. Give me a project that was an efficiency success and a business failure. Now the reverse.
4. If the iron triangle is inadequate, why is it still on every slide deck in the industry?
5. PMBOK went from 49 processes → 0 → 40 in eight years. What problem was each swing solving?
6. Which of these four documents could you actually sue someone over? Why does that matter?
7. The Scrum Guide says Scrum is "purposefully incomplete." What is it incomplete *about*, and who fills the gap?
8. Your organization mandates PRINCE2 and your team wants Scrum. Name the specific artifacts that collide.
:::

::: {.editor}
### Editor challenge — attack these claims

> "Because 99.5% of large projects miss at least one of budget, schedule, or benefits, the discipline of project management has essentially failed."

Lines of attack: selection effects in the database; the counterfactual is unmeasured — how bad would
these projects be *without* project management?; "benefits shortfall" depends on who wrote the
business case; the Scandinavian data contradicts universality; the base rate mixes project types with
wildly different uncertainty.

> "Standards bodies revise their frameworks primarily to sell new certifications, not because knowledge advanced."

This one is uncomfortable and partly defensible. Separate the cynical claim (revenue motive) from the
testable one (did practice improve?). The Scrum Guide — free, and unrevised for six years — is the
counterexample that complicates the cynical reading.
:::
